papers.title: A morphology-aware process–structure–property framework for SLM AlSi10Mg: Decoupling grain and dendrite contributions
papers.abstract: • Develop an automated multi-scale PSP framework for AM process optimization. • Integrate ML and physics simulation to build an interpretable process map. • Separate microstructure predictors from misleading proxies for performance. • Identify equiaxed fraction as the dominant yield strength predictor. • Confirm that dendrite morphology is a misleading proxy for hardness. Establishing a robust process–structure–property (PSP) framework is critical for designing additively manufactured (AM) alloys with tailored performance. Here we introduce a morphology-aware PSP workflow for SLM AlSi10Mg that, for the first time, enables systematic quantification of dendritic/cellular morphologies by reconstructing the Si network into closed cells. This high-throughput approach, combined with EBSD grain analysis, thermophysical modelling, and validated statistics, allows direct comparison of grain- and dendrite-level predictors. We show that grain classification (equiaxed vs. columnar) refines the Hall–Petch relation and reliably predicts yield strength. In contrast, while dendritic morphology is widely assumed to correlate with hardness, it fails as a predictor. Moreover, this work presents direct microstructural evidence for decoupling between grains and dendrites. For instance, in the melt pool boundary region, columnar grains are predominantly filled with equiaxed dendrites. This indicates that the final dendritic morphology is more strongly influenced by local solidification conditions than by the parent grain it resides in. The proposed framework is potentially transferable to other AM alloys with cellular or dendritic microstructures (e.g., SLM Ti-6Al-4V, IN718) and highlights the risk of relying on visually intuitive but statistically unsupported proxies in PSP framework.

summary_en.motivation: To establish a robust process-structure-property framework for optimizing additively manufactured alloys.

papers.title: Microstructure and Properties of Gas-Nitrided Ti-6Al-4V Alloy
papers.abstract: To enhance its surface properties, the Ti-6Al-4V alloy was subjected to a nitrogen atmosphere at elevated temperatures. An orthogonal experiment was employed to investigate the effects of nitriding temperature, nitriding duration, and nitrogen flow rate on the surface hardness and the thickness of the nitrided layer. Mechanical properties were assessed using a micro-Vickers hardness tester and a universal material testing machine. Accelerated corrosion tests were performed by immersing the samples in solutions with varying HF concentrations, while wear resistance was evaluated via a circumferential dry sliding wear test. The results indicate that after nitriding, the subsurface region is primarily composed of TiN, Ti2N, and Ti2AlN. Nitriding temperature exerts the greatest influence on the thickness of the nitrided layer, whereas nitrogen flow rate has the least impact. Conversely, nitrogen flow rate shows the strongest effect on surface hardness, with nitriding temperature having the weakest influence. After nitriding, the microstructure becomes coarse with a decrease in substrate hardness. As nitriding temperature and time increase, the thickness of the nitrided layer grows, but both the tensile strength and percentage elongation after fracture decline. The sample nitrided at 850 °C for 2 h under a nitrogen flow rate of 20 mL·min−1 exhibits favorable overall properties. Compared with the as-received sample, its surface hardness increases noticeably, though both the tensile strength and percentage elongation after fracture decrease. In comparison to the continuous weight loss of the as-received sample when immersed in HF solution, the nitrided sample exhibits an initial mass loss of nearly zero, which suggests that the nitrided layer has a protective efficacy. After nitriding, the wear rate is reduced to no more than 3% of that of the as-received sample. Therefore, gas nitriding is considered a feasible technique for improving the surface properties of Ti-6Al-4V in complex environments.

summary_en.motivation: To improve the surface properties of Ti-6Al-4V alloy through gas nitriding.
summary_en.method: Orthogonal experiments varying nitriding temperature, duration, and nitrogen flow rate were conducted, followed by microhardness, tensile, corrosion, and wear tests.
summary_en.result: Gas nitriding increased surface hardness and wear resistance but reduced tensile strength and elongation, with best overall properties at 850°C for 2h.
summary_en.validation: Mechanical testing (micro-Vickers hardness, universal testing machine), immersion corrosion tests, and dry sliding wear tests.
